m3-l001-vectors-matrices.prompt: For a matrix $A$ and vector $x$, which statement about $Ax=b$ is correct?
options: Solvable exactly when $b$ is in the span of the rows of $A$.
Solvable exactly when $b$ is in the span of the columns of $A$.
Solvable exactly when $b$ is perpendicular to every column of $A$.
Solvable whenever $A$ has at least as many rows as columns.
m3-l001-vectors-matrices.explanation: $Ax = x_1\,\text{col}_1 + \dots + x_n\,\text{col}_n$, so $Ax=b$ asks whether $b$ is a linear combination of the columns, and $x$ lists the coefficients. Row spans and shapes alone do not decide solvability.

m3-l001-vectors-matrices.prompt: The vectors $v_1=(1,0,2)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$, $v_3=(1,1,3)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are given. What is their span?
options: All of $\mathbb{R}^3$, because three vectors always span three-dimensional space.
A line through the origin, because all three vectors have positive entries.
A plane that misses the origin.
A plane through the origin, because $v_3=v_1+v_2$ adds nothing new.
m3-l001-vectors-matrices.explanation: Since $v_3 = v_1 + v_2$, the third vector is already in the span of the first two. Counting vectors does not give the dimension; only independent directions count. A span always contains the zero vector.

m3-l001-vectors-matrices.prompt: Find the angle in degrees between $u=(1,2,2)$ and $v=(3,0,4)$. Give the answer in degrees.
m3-l001-vectors-matrices.explanation: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{u\cdot v}{|u||v|} = \dfrac{11}{3\cdot 5}=\dfrac{11}{15}$, so $\theta \approx 42.8^\circ$. Cauchy-Schwarz guarantees this ratio is between $-1$ and $1$.

m3-l001-vectors-matrices.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=(3,-1)$. Compute $Ax$ as $3\,\text{col}_1 - 1\,\text{col}_2$ and give its third component.
m3-l001-vectors-matrices.explanation: $Ax = 3(2,1,0) - (1,3,4) = (5,0,-4)$. The third component is $-4$: the column view builds $Ax$ one column at a time.

m3-l001-vectors-matrices.prompt: In your own words, explain why viewing $Ax$ as a combination of the columns of $A$ is the picture that generalises, and what question $Ax=b$ is asking in that picture.
m3-l001-vectors-matrices.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $Ax$ is a sum of columns weighted by the entries of $x$; (2) the set of all $Ax$ is the span of the columns (the column space), so $Ax=b$ asks whether $b$ is in that span; (3) a reason it generalises (works for any shape, leads to subspaces and rank, whereas row dot products are just one way to compute entries).
m3-l001-vectors-matrices.modelAnswer: Each entry of $x$ is the amount of one column of $A$ you mix in, so $Ax$ is a recipe for building a vector from the columns. Every possible output is therefore a point in the span of the columns, and $Ax=b$ asks whether the target $b$ can be built from those ingredients. This view carries over to any matrix shape and leads straight to column space, rank and basis, while the row-by-row dot-product view only tells you how to compute one number at a time.

m3-l002-geometry-elimination.prompt: The system $x+y=2$, $2x+2y=5$ is solved by elimination. What happens and what does it mean?
options: Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives $0=1$, so the system is inconsistent and has no solution.
Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives $0=0$, so there are infinitely many solutions.
Elimination produces two pivots, so the solution is unique and easy to find.
A solution must exist, because there are as many equations as unknowns here.
m3-l002-geometry-elimination.explanation: Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives $0x+0y = 1$. A missing pivot with an inconsistent right-hand side means the two lines are parallel and never meet. Square shape does not guarantee a solution; the pivots decide.

m3-l002-geometry-elimination.prompt: After elimination on a $3\times3$ system you reach a final row $(0\;0\;0\,|\,0)$ and only two pivots. What does the row picture show?
options: Three planes meet at exactly one point.
The three planes have no common point, because a row of zeros appeared.
Three planes share a whole line of solutions, with one free variable.
Two planes are identical and the third is parallel to them, so no solution exists.
m3-l002-geometry-elimination.explanation: The last equation reads $0=0$, so it is consistent but carries no information: one free variable remains and the planes share a line. A contradictory row like $(0\;0\;0\,|\,1)$ would instead mean no solution.

m3-l002-geometry-elimination.prompt: Eliminate on $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&-6&0\\-2&7&2\end{pmatrix}$ (no row exchanges). What is the third pivot?
m3-l002-geometry-elimination.explanation: Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2 (multiplier 2) and $-1$ times row 1 from row 3. Then row 3 minus $(-1)$ times row 2 gives the pivot $1$. The pivots are $2,-8,1$.

m3-l002-geometry-elimination.prompt: For the same matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&-6&0\\-2&7&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is the multiplier $\ell_{32}$ used to clear the $(3,2)$ position after the first column is cleared?
m3-l002-geometry-elimination.explanation: After step one, rows 2 and 3 are $(0,-8,-2)$ and $(0,8,3)$, so $\ell_{32} = 8/(-8) = -1$. Each multiplier becomes an entry of $E_{32}$ (and later of $L$).

m3-l002-geometry-elimination.prompt: Explain how a $2\times 2$ system looks in the row picture and in the column picture, and how elimination (done as multiplication by elementary matrices $E_{ij}$) tells you which of the three outcomes occurs.
m3-l002-geometry-elimination.rubric: Full credit requires: row picture = two lines meeting (or not); column picture = combining column vectors to reach the right-hand side; elimination step = left-multiplication by $E_{ij}$ with the multiplier; pivots decide outcome: full pivots -> unique, missing pivot with inconsistent row -> none, missing pivot with consistent row -> infinitely many.
m3-l002-geometry-elimination.modelAnswer: In the row picture each equation is a line and the solution is where they cross; in the column picture the two columns are vectors and we ask what mix of them reaches the right side. Each elimination step subtracts a multiple of one row from another, which is multiplication by an elementary matrix $E_{ij}$ holding that multiplier. If we get a full set of pivots the solution is unique; if a pivot is missing we either hit a contradiction like $0=1$ (no solution, parallel lines) or $0=0$ (a free variable, infinitely many solutions).

m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.prompt: Rotate a book $90^\circ$ about the $x$-axis and then $90^\circ$ about the $y$-axis. Doing the two rotations in the opposite order gives a different final orientation. What does this show?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative, which is why the order of rotations matters.
Finite rotations commute, so the different results must come from sloppy rotating.
Rotation matrices do not commute, so $AB\ne BA$, although multiplication is associative.
The final orientations agree, because both orders rotate through the same total angle.
m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.explanation: Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative, and 3D rotations are the standard physical example. This non-commutativity underlies angular-momentum commutators later on.

m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.prompt: If $A$ and $B$ are invertible, which expression equals $(AB)^{-1}$?
options: $B^{-1}A^{-1}$, since the last operation applied must be undone first.
$A^{-1}B^{-1}$, since inverses can be applied in whichever order is convenient.
$A^{-1}+B^{-1}$, since the inverse of a product splits into a sum of inverses.
$(A+B)^{-1}$, since the inverse of a product equals the inverse of the sum.
m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.explanation: $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A(BB^{-1})A^{-1} = I$. The order reverses because the last operation applied must be the first one undone.

m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.prompt: Using Gauss-Jordan elimination (or the $2\times2$ formula), find the $(2,1)$ entry of $A^{-1}$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\7&6\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.explanation: $\det A = 24-14 = 10$ and $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix}6&-2\\-7&4\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(2,1)$ entry is $-0.7$.

m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(2,2)$ entry of $AB$.
m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.explanation: Row 2 of $A$ times column 2 of $B$: $3\cdot1 + 4\cdot2 = 11$. Equivalently $AB=\sum_k(\text{col}_k A)(\text{row}_k B)$, whose $(2,2)$ entry is $3\cdot1+4\cdot2$.

m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.prompt: Why does the order reverse in $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$, and how can you tell from the pivots (Gauss-Jordan) whether a square matrix has an inverse?
m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.rubric: Full credit requires: an everyday or algebraic argument for reversal (undo the last step first; verify $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=I$); and that an inverse exists iff elimination produces $n$ pivots (Gauss-Jordan turns $[A\,|\,I]$ into $[I\,|\,A^{-1}]$), failing when a pivot is missing.
m3-l003-matrix-ops-inverses.modelAnswer: If $AB$ means 'do $B$, then $A$', undoing it requires first undoing $A$ and then undoing $B$, giving $B^{-1}A^{-1}$ (put on socks, then shoes; remove shoes first). Algebraically $AB\,B^{-1}A^{-1}=A\,I\,A^{-1}=I$. For existence, run Gauss-Jordan on $[A\,|\,I]$: if you get $n$ pivots you can reduce the left block to $I$ and the right block is $A^{-1}$; a missing pivot means the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

m3-l004-lu-transposes.prompt: In $A=LU$ (no row exchanges), why can the multipliers be written into $L$ exactly as they were used, with no mixing?
options: $L$ is the product of the elimination matrices $E_{ij}$ themselves, in the order applied.
The multipliers are stored in $U$, and $L$ is simply the identity matrix here.
$L$ holds the pivots, which never change during elimination, so no mixing arises.
$L$ is built from the inverse steps in reverse order, which do not interact.
m3-l004-lu-transposes.explanation: $E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A=U$ gives $A=E_{21}^{-1}E_{31}^{-1}E_{32}^{-1}U$. Each inverse just flips the sign of its multiplier, and in this order the multipliers drop into $L$ directly. The product of the $E$ themselves would mix them.

m3-l004-lu-transposes.prompt: You must solve $Ax=b$ for 1000 different right-hand sides with the same large $A$. What is the efficient strategy?
options: Run full Gaussian elimination again for each new $b$, since the multipliers depend on $b$.
Factor $A=LU$ once (about $n^3/3$ operations), then do a forward and a back substitution per $b$ (about $n^2$).
Refactor $A$ for every $b$, because $L$ and $U$ change when the right-hand side changes.
Compute $A^{-1}$ from scratch for every $b$, since only an inverse can be reused.
m3-l004-lu-transposes.explanation: The factorisation depends only on $A$, not on $b$. After the one-time $n^3/3$ cost, each solve costs about $n^2$ for the two triangular solves.

m3-l004-lu-transposes.prompt: Use $A=LU$ to solve $Ax=b$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&-6&0\\-2&7&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=(5,-2,9)$. Give $x_3$.
m3-l004-lu-transposes.explanation: Forward substitution $Lc=b$ gives $c=(5,-12,2)$, then back substitution $Ux=c$ gives $x=(1,1,2)$, so $x_3=2$.

m3-l004-lu-transposes.prompt: LU factorisation costs about $n^3/3$ operations. If a factorisation of an $n=100$ matrix takes 1 s, how many seconds does an $n=400$ matrix take?
m3-l004-lu-transposes.explanation: The cost scales as $n^3$, so quadrupling $n$ multiplies the time by $4^3=64$. This is why dense linear algebra gets expensive fast.

m3-l004-lu-transposes.prompt: What goes wrong when a zero pivot appears, how do row exchanges fix it (giving $PA=LU$), and why is $P^{-1}=P^T$ for a permutation matrix?
m3-l004-lu-transposes.rubric: Full credit requires: a zero pivot blocks elimination in that position, but a nonzero entry below can be swapped up if $A$ is invertible; $P$ records the swaps; $P$ has orthonormal columns (one 1 per row/column) so $P^TP=I$.
m3-l004-lu-transposes.modelAnswer: If a pivot position holds zero, you cannot divide by it, but if the matrix is invertible some row below has a nonzero entry in that column; exchanging rows brings it up. The permutation matrix $P$ records all these swaps so that $PA=LU$ works. A permutation matrix has a single 1 in each row and column, so its columns are orthonormal and $P^TP=I$, meaning $P^{-1}=P^T$.

m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.prompt: Which of these subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a subspace?
options: The plane $x+y+z=0$, which contains the origin and is closed under sums.
The plane $x+y+z=1$, since it is also a flat sheet in space.
The first octant ($x,y,z\ge0$), since sums of its vectors stay inside it.
The unit sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$, since it is symmetric about the origin.
m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.explanation: A subspace must contain $0$ and be closed under addition and scaling. $x+y+z=0$ passes both tests; the shifted plane misses the origin, the octant fails under multiplication by $-1$, and the sphere fails both.

options: $b=(1,2,4)$, since any vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be reached by two columns.
$b=(1,1,1)$, since it is perpendicular to the nullspace of $A$.
$b=(2,4,6)$, which equals $2(1,2,3)$ and so lies on the line spanned by both columns.
$b=(3,2,1)$, since its entries sum to 6, like the first column's entries.
m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.explanation: Both columns are multiples of $(1,2,3)$, so $C(A)$ is that line only. $(2,4,6)=2(1,2,3)$ is on it; the other vectors are not.

m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.prompt: Find the dimension of the nullspace of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3&4\\2&4&6&8\\1&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.explanation: Row 2 is twice row 1, so the rank is 2 and there are $4-2=2$ free variables, so $\dim N(A)=2$.

m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.prompt: The reduced row echelon form of $A$ is $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&3&0&2\\0&0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$. The special solution with free variables $x_2=0$, $x_4=1$ has what value of $x_3$?
m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.explanation: Set the free variables, then read off the pivot variables from $R$: $x_3=-4x_4=-4$ and $x_1=-3x_2-2x_4=-2$. So the special solution is $(-2,0,-4,1)$.

m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.prompt: Explain what the nullspace of $A$ tells you about the columns of $A$, why it is a subspace, and how the reduced form $R$ lets you read off its special solutions.
m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.rubric: Full credit requires: $x\in N(A)$ means a combination of the columns equals zero (so nonzero nullspace = dependent columns); closure under addition and scaling follows from linearity; free variables are set to 1/0 one at a time and the pivot variables are read off R (negatives of the free column entries).
m3-l005-subspaces-nullspace.modelAnswer: A vector in the nullspace is a recipe for combining the columns of $A$ to get zero, so a nonzero nullspace means the columns are dependent. If $Ax=0$ and $Ay=0$ then $A(x+y)=0$ and $A(cx)=0$, so it is a subspace. In the reduced form $R$ each free column is a combination of the pivot columns; setting one free variable to 1 (others 0) and moving the pivot-column entries to the other side with a minus sign gives the special solutions, and all of $N(A)$ is their combinations.

m3-l006-complete-solution.prompt: $A$ is a $3\times5$ matrix with rank 3. What can you say about $Ax=b$?
options: Exactly one solution for every $b$, because the rank equals the number of equations.
It is always solvable (rank 3 equals the number of rows), with 2 free parameters in the complete solution.
Solvable only for some $b$, because there are more unknowns than equations.
Exactly two solutions for every $b$, one for each of the free variables.
m3-l006-complete-solution.explanation: Rank $3 = m$ means the columns span all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (always solvable) and $n-r=2$ free variables give a 2-parameter family $x_p+c_1s_1+c_2s_2$.

m3-l006-complete-solution.prompt: Balancing $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6+a\,\text{O}_2\to b\,\text{CO}_2+c\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$ means finding the nullspace of the element-balance matrix. It has 3 rows (C, H, O) and 4 species columns and rank 3. What does that imply?
options: No balanced reaction exists, because the rank equals the number of elements.
Three independent balanced reactions exist, one for each element balanced.
A unique balanced reaction exists whose integer coefficients cannot be scaled at all.
The nullspace is one-dimensional: one balanced reaction exists, up to scale.
m3-l006-complete-solution.explanation: $\dim N = n-r = 4-3 = 1$. Any multiple of the balanced equation is also balanced, which is why we fix the scale by demanding smallest integers.

m3-l006-complete-solution.prompt: Solve $Ax=b$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&3&1&2\\0&0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1,6)$, with the free variables $x_2=x_4=0$ (a particular solution). Give $x_1$.
m3-l006-complete-solution.explanation: With $x_2=x_4=0$: $x_3=6$ from row 2, then $x_1+x_3=1$ gives $x_1=-5$. Adding any nullspace vector gives the complete solution.

m3-l006-complete-solution.prompt: Balance $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6+a\,\text{O}_2\to 2\,\text{CO}_2+3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$. How many moles of $\text{O}_2$ per mole of ethane ($a$)?
m3-l006-complete-solution.explanation: Oxygen atoms: $2a = 2\cdot2+3 = 7$, so $a=3.5$. This is the nullspace vector $(1,3.5,2,3)$ of the balance matrix, scaled so ethane has coefficient 1.

m3-l006-complete-solution.prompt: Explain why the complete solution to $Ax=b$ has the form $x=x_p+x_n$, and how the rank decides both solvability and the number of free parameters.
m3-l006-complete-solution.rubric: Full credit requires: $A(x_p+x_n)=b+0$ and any two solutions differ by a nullspace vector; rank = number of pivots; solvable for all b if r=m, free parameters = n-r.
m3-l006-complete-solution.modelAnswer: If $x_p$ solves $Ax=b$ and $x_n$ satisfies $Ax_n=0$, then $A(x_p+x_n)=b$; conversely the difference of two solutions is in the nullspace, so all solutions are $x_p$ plus the nullspace. The rank $r$ counts independent pivots: if $r=m$ every $b$ is reachable, otherwise only $b$ in the column space; and there are $n-r$ free variables, which sets the size of the family of solutions.

m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.prompt: You have four vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Which statement is true?
options: They are independent as long as no two of them are parallel to each other.
They must be dependent, since the $3\times4$ matrix has a free column.
They are independent provided none of them is the zero vector itself.
They can form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, since a basis may have any size.
m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.explanation: Independence means $N(A)=\{0\}$. With $n=4>m=3$ there are at most 3 pivots, hence at least one free variable. Pairwise non-parallel is not enough, and every basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ has exactly 3 vectors.

m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.prompt: After row reduction $A\to R$, a basis for the column space $C(A)$ is formed by:
options: The pivot columns of $R$, because row operations preserve the column space.
The pivot rows of $R$, rewritten as column vectors instead of rows.
The special solutions of $Ax=0$, which span the same space as the columns.
The columns of the original $A$ in the pivot positions, not those of $R$.
m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.explanation: Row operations preserve the row space and the nullspace, but they change the column space (the columns of $R$ have different entries). The pivot positions tell you which original columns are independent.

m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.prompt: Find the dimension of the span of $(1,0,1)$, $(1,1,2)$ and $(0,1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.explanation: The third vector equals the second minus the first, so only two are independent: rank 2, a plane.

m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.prompt: A $3\times5$ matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0&1&3\\0&0&1&2&1\\1&2&1&3&4\end{pmatrix}$ has row 3 = row 1 + row 2. What is the dimension of its nullspace?
m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.explanation: Rank is 2, so $\dim N(A)=5-2=3$. The row space and column space both have dimension 2.

m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.prompt: What is a basis, why does every basis of a given space contain the same number of vectors, and how does rank relate to the dimensions of the row space and column space?
m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.rubric: Full credit requires: basis = independent and spanning; same size (dimension) because more vectors than the dimension would be dependent and fewer cannot span; rank = number of pivots = dim C(A) = dim C(A^T).
m3-l007-independence-basis-dim.modelAnswer: A basis is a set of vectors that is independent (no redundancy) and spans the space (reaches everything). If one basis had more vectors than another, the extra ones would have to be dependent, and if it had fewer it could not span, so all bases have the same size, which defines the dimension. The rank is the number of pivots, and it equals both the dimension of the column space and of the row space.

m3-l008-four-subspaces.prompt: Row-reducing $A$ to $R=EA$ leaves some zero rows at the bottom of $R$. The matching rows of $E$ give a basis for which subspace?
options: The left nullspace $N(A^T)$, since each such row $y^T$ satisfies $y^TA=0$.
The nullspace $N(A)$, because the zero rows of $R$ show which inputs vanish.
The column space $C(A)$, because those rows of $E$ come directly from $A$.
The row space $C(A^T)$, because row operations never change the row space.
m3-l008-four-subspaces.explanation: A zero row of $EA$ means $(\text{row of }E)\cdot A=0$, i.e. a vector with $y^TA=0$. These are exactly the left-nullspace vectors, and there are $m-r$ of them.

m3-l008-four-subspaces.prompt: A reaction network has 6 species and its element-balance matrix has rank 3. How many independent balanced reactions (independent vectors of stoichiometric coefficients) can exist?
options: 6, one independent reaction for every species in the network.
9, the number of species plus the rank of the balance matrix.
3, the nullspace dimension $n-r=6-3$, one for each free variable.
0, because six unknowns cannot satisfy three constraints at once.
m3-l008-four-subspaces.explanation: Balanced reactions are vectors with balance matrix times coefficients $=0$, so they form the nullspace of dimension $n-r = 6-3 = 3$.

m3-l008-four-subspaces.prompt: A $5\times8$ matrix has rank 3. What is the dimension of its left nullspace $N(A^T)$?
m3-l008-four-subspaces.explanation: $\dim N(A^T)=m-r=5-3=2$. Together: $\dim C(A)=3$, $\dim N(A)=5$, $\dim C(A^T)=3$, $\dim N(A^T)=2$.

m3-l008-four-subspaces.prompt: A $100\times100$ matrix of rank 2 can be written as a sum of two rank-one pieces (column times row). How many numbers must you store for this representation?
m3-l008-four-subspaces.explanation: Each rank-1 piece $uv^T$ needs $100+100=200$ numbers, so two pieces need 400 instead of 10,000 for the full matrix. This is the idea behind low-rank compression.

m3-l008-four-subspaces.prompt: In your own words, explain why $r+(n-r)=n$ and how the four fundamental subspaces pair up inside $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$.
m3-l008-four-subspaces.rubric: Full credit requires: each of the $n$ input directions is either a pivot direction (carried to the column space, $r$ of them) or a free direction (sent to zero, $n-r$); row space (dim r) + nullspace (dim n-r) fill $\mathbb{R}^n$; column space (r) + left nullspace (m-r) fill $\mathbb{R}^m$.
m3-l008-four-subspaces.modelAnswer: Of the $n$ columns, $r$ are pivot columns that give independent directions and $n-r$ are free columns that can be expressed in terms of them. The free columns are what give the nullspace dimension $n-r$, so rank plus nullity counts all $n$ inputs. On the input side the row space (dimension $r$) and nullspace (dimension $n-r$) together account for $\mathbb{R}^n$; on the output side the column space ($r$) and left nullspace ($m-r$) together account for $\mathbb{R}^m$.

m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.prompt: Why is every vector in the nullspace of $A$ perpendicular to every row of $A$ (and to the whole row space)?
options: The rows of $A$ are always independent of each other, so they sit at right angles.
The nullspace is defined as the set of vectors perpendicular to the columns.
$Ax=0$ says every row dotted with $x$ is zero, so $x$ is perpendicular to all rows.
$A$ is assumed to be an orthogonal matrix, so its rows and columns are perpendicular.
m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.explanation: Reading $Ax=0$ row by row gives $\text{row}_i\cdot x=0$ for every $i$. The row space is spanned by these rows, so $x$ is perpendicular to all of it.

m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.prompt: $A$ is $5\times3$ and its columns are linearly dependent. What can you say about the $3\times3$ matrix $A^TA$?
options: It is singular, since $A^TA$ has the same nullspace as $A$.
It is invertible, since any square symmetric matrix has an inverse.
It is invertible, since $A^T$ has independent rows even when $A$ does not.
It is undefined, since $A$ is not square and cannot be multiplied by $A^T$.
m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.explanation: If $Ax=0$ then $A^TAx=0$, and conversely $A^TAx=0\Rightarrow x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|^2=0$. So $N(A^TA)=N(A)$, and $A^TA$ is invertible exactly when $A$ has independent columns.

m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.prompt: Take $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=(3,1)$. Split $x=x_r+x_n$ (row-space part plus nullspace part). Give the length $|x_n|$ of the nullspace component.
m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.explanation: The row space is the line through $(1,1)$: $x_r=(2,2)$. The remainder $x_n=(1,-1)$ satisfies $Ax_n=0$, with length $\sqrt2\approx1.414$. $A$ sends $x$ to $Ax=4=Ax_r$; the nullspace part is invisible to $A$.

m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.prompt: For $a=(1,2,2)$ spanning a line, give the length of the component of $x=(1,1,1)$ along $a$.
m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.explanation: $\dfrac{a\cdot x}{|a|}=\dfrac{5}{3}\approx1.667$. This is the length of the projection of $x$ onto the line.

m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.prompt: Describe what a matrix $A$ does to the row-space part and to the nullspace part of an input vector $x$, and why this means each output $b$ in the column space has exactly one row-space preimage.
m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.rubric: Full credit requires: $x=x_r+x_n$ with $x_r\perp x_n$; $A x_n = 0$ so only $x_r$ matters; $A$ maps the row space one-to-one onto the column space (invertible between them), so each $b$ in $C(A)$ comes from exactly one row-space vector.
m3-l009-orthogonal-subspaces.modelAnswer: Every input splits uniquely into a row-space piece and a nullspace piece that are perpendicular. $A$ annihilates the nullspace piece and carries the row-space piece to the output. Within the row space, $A$ is a one-to-one map onto the column space (both have dimension $r$), so each reachable output $b$ comes from exactly one vector in the row space, with all other solutions differing by a nullspace vector.

m3-l010-projections-least-squares.prompt: In a least-squares fit $\min\|Ax-b\|^2$, what is true of the residual $e=b-A\hat x$?
options: It is parallel to $b$, since the fit just rescales the data vector.
It lies inside the column space of $A$.
It is the shortest vector with all of its components equal to each other.
It is perpendicular to every column of $A$, so $A^Te=0$.
m3-l010-projections-least-squares.explanation: The closest point $p=A\hat x$ in $C(A)$ is the projection of $b$, so the error $b-p$ is perpendicular to $C(A)$. That is $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$, the normal equations.

m3-l010-projections-least-squares.prompt: A projection matrix satisfies $P^2=P$. What is the physical or geometric reason?
options: $P$ is symmetric, and symmetry alone forces $P^2=P$ for every matrix.
After one projection the vector is already in the subspace.
Projecting twice returns the original vector, so $P$ undoes itself.
Every projection matrix has determinant 1.
m3-l010-projections-least-squares.explanation: $Pb$ is in $C(A)$, and $P$ leaves every vector of $C(A)$ unchanged. (Symmetry is a separate property, giving orthogonal projection, and a singular $P$ has determinant 0 unless $P=I$.)

m3-l010-projections-least-squares.prompt: Fit a line $y=C+Dt$ by least squares to the points $(1,1),(2,2),(3,2),(4,4)$. Give the slope $D$.
m3-l010-projections-least-squares.explanation: Solving $A^TA\hat x=A^Ty$ for $A=[1\;t]$ gives $C=0$, $D=0.9$ (the line passes through the origin). The residual vector is perpendicular to both the column of ones and the column $t$.

m3-l010-projections-least-squares.prompt: A Beer-Lambert calibration through the origin $A_{\rm bs}=\varepsilon\ell\,c$ has data $c=0.1,0.2,0.4$ mM and absorbance $0.12,0.25,0.47$. Using one-column least squares, find $\varepsilon\ell$ in mM$^{-1}$.
m3-l010-projections-least-squares.explanation: The projection onto a single column gives $\hat x=\dfrac{c\cdot A_{\rm bs}}{c\cdot c}=\dfrac{0.250}{0.21}\approx 1.190$ mM$^{-1}$. Calibration slopes are projections.

m3-l010-projections-least-squares.prompt: Explain in your own words why minimising $\|Ax-b\|^2$ leads to the normal equations $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$ and why this is a projection of $b$ onto the column space. Why is a calibration curve an example?
m3-l010-projections-least-squares.rubric: Full credit requires: closest point in a subspace is where the error is perpendicular to it; this gives $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$; the fitted values $A\hat x$ are the projection of the data vector onto the span of the model columns; calibration: data vector projected onto span{ones, concentration}.
m3-l010-projections-least-squares.modelAnswer: The set of all achievable predictions $Ax$ is the column space of $A$. The point in that subspace closest to the data $b$ is found by dropping a perpendicular, so the leftover error must be perpendicular to every column: $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$, i.e. $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$. A calibration fit has columns (ones, concentrations); the measured absorbances form a vector in a higher-dimensional space, and the fitted line is its projection onto the plane spanned by those columns.

m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.prompt: If $Q$ has orthonormal columns and is square, what does multiplying a vector by $Q$ do?
options: It preserves lengths and angles (a rotation or reflection), since $Q^TQ=I$.
It preserves lengths but can change angles between different vectors.
It makes the components of any vector orthogonal to one another.
It scales every length by the factor $\det Q$ for any input vector.
m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.explanation: $Q^TQ=I$ gives $(Qx)\cdot(Qy)=x\cdot y$, so lengths and angles are unchanged. Also $\det Q=\pm1$, but that is a sign (orientation), not a scale factor.

m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.prompt: In $A=QR$ from Gram-Schmidt, why is $R$ upper triangular?
options: Gram-Schmidt processes the rows of $A$ from the bottom up to the top.
$R$ equals $Q^T$, and $Q$ happens to be lower triangular.
$q_k$ uses only $a_1,\dots,a_k$, so $a_k$ has no later $q_j$ parts.
The entries below the diagonal are cancelled to keep $Q$ orthogonal.
m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.explanation: Each new $q_k$ lies in span$\{a_1..a_k\}$, hence each $a_k$ is a combination of $q_1..q_k$ only. The coefficients $r_{jk}=q_j^Ta_k$ vanish for $j>k$.

m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.prompt: Apply Gram-Schmidt to $a_1=(1,1,0)$, $a_2=(1,0,1)$. In $A=QR$, what is $r_{22}$ (the length of the part of $a_2$ left after removing the $q_1$ component)?
With orthonormal columns, least squares is simply $\hat x=Q^Tb$. For $q_1=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2$ and $b=(2,4,6)$, give $\hat x_1=q_1\cdot b$.
m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.explanation: $\hat x_1=(2+4)/\sqrt2=6/\sqrt2\approx4.243$. With orthonormal columns each coefficient is found independently, with no system to solve.

m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.prompt: Why does orthonormality make least-squares fitting almost trivial, and what does the matrix $R$ in $A=QR$ record?
m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.rubric: Full credit requires: with $Q^TQ=I$, $A^TA$ becomes $I$ so $\hat x=Q^Tb$ (each coefficient is a dot product); R records the dot products $q_j^Ta_k$ (the Gram-Schmidt coefficients) and lengths, expressing the original columns in the new orthonormal basis.
m3-l011-gram-schmidt-qr.modelAnswer: If the columns are orthonormal, $Q^TQ=I$, so the normal equations $Q^TQ\hat x=Q^Tb$ collapse to $\hat x=Q^Tb$: each coefficient is just the dot product of $b$ with one basis vector, with no coupling between them. In $A=QR$, Gram-Schmidt rewrites each original column $a_k$ in terms of the new orthonormal vectors, and $R$ stores those coefficients: the off-diagonal entries are the components removed, and the diagonal entries are the lengths of what was left.

m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ has $\det A=5$. What is $\det(2A)$?
options: $10$, because doubling the matrix just doubles its determinant.
$40$, since each of the 3 rows doubles and the determinant is linear in each: $2^3\cdot5$.
$25$, because the determinant is squared when the matrix is doubled.
$30$, because each of the three rows adds 1 to the scaling factor.
m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.explanation: The determinant is linear in each row separately, so scaling all 3 rows by 2 multiplies it by $2^3=8$: $8\cdot5=40$. In general $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$.

m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.prompt: Why does $\det A=0$ exactly when $A$ is not invertible?
options: The determinant counts the nonzero entries, so it vanishes only for the zero matrix.
It measures how far $A$ is from symmetric, and singular matrices are skew.
It is defined as the largest eigenvalue.
$\det A=\pm$ product of pivots, and a singular matrix lacks a pivot.
m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.explanation: Elimination reduces $A$ to $U$ with $\det A=\pm\prod(\text{pivots})$ (the sign from row exchanges). A zero pivot means a dependent row, so $A$ is singular and the product vanishes.
The pivots are $2,-8,1$, with no row exchanges, so $\det A=2\cdot(-8)\cdot1=-16$.

m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.prompt: If $\det A=-16$ and $\det B=12$ for $3\times3$ matrices, what is $\det(A^{-1}B)$?
m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.explanation: $\det(A^{-1}B)=\det(A^{-1})\det B=\dfrac{12}{-16}=-0.75$, using $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ and $\det A^{-1}=1/\det A$.

m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.prompt: State the three defining properties of the determinant and show how they imply that a row exchange flips the sign and that $\det A=0$ for a matrix with two equal rows.
m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.rubric: Full credit requires: det I = 1; sign flips on exchange (or: linear in each row separately); stated consequences: two equal rows -> exchanging them changes nothing but flips sign, so det = -det = 0.
m3-l012-det-properties-formulas.modelAnswer: The defining properties are: (1) $\det I = 1$; (2) the sign reverses when two rows are exchanged; (3) the determinant is linear in each row separately. If two rows are equal, exchanging them leaves the matrix unchanged but must flip the sign of the determinant, so $\det A=-\det A$, giving $\det A=0$. Row-subtraction then shows the determinant is unchanged by elimination, so it equals the product of the pivots.

m3-l013-cramer-volume.prompt: Why is Cramer's rule rarely used to solve large linear systems numerically?
options: It only works for $2\times2$ systems, since larger determinants are undefined.
It needs $n+1$ determinants, each costing about one full elimination.
It gives wrong answers whenever the determinant is small but nonzero.
It requires the coefficient matrix to be symmetric and positive definite.
m3-l013-cramer-volume.explanation: Cramer's rule is exact and useful for formulas and small cases (symbolic work), but computing all those determinants is wasteful; elimination (LU) solves the system with a single factorisation.

m3-l013-cramer-volume.prompt: Why does the Jacobian determinant appear when you change variables in a multiple integral, e.g. $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$?
options: It is the average of the partial derivatives over the small region.
It makes the new coordinates orthogonal to the original ones.
It matters only for linear maps, never for curved coordinate systems.
It is the local factor by which the map scales area or volume.
m3-l013-cramer-volume.explanation: A smooth map is locally linear (the Jacobian matrix) and $|\det|$ of a linear map is the volume scale factor. In polar coordinates $|\det J|=r$ because arc length grows with radius.

m3-l013-cramer-volume.prompt: Find the volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are the rows $(1,2,0)$, $(0,1,3)$, $(2,0,1)$.
Explain geometrically why $|\det A|$ is the volume of the box spanned by the columns, and what $\det A=0$ says about that box.
m3-l013-cramer-volume.rubric: Full credit requires: $|\det A|$ = volume of parallelepiped (unit cube maps to it); sign = orientation; zero determinant = columns dependent so the box is flat (zero volume, lies in a lower-dimensional space), consistent with singular matrix.
m3-l013-cramer-volume.modelAnswer: $A$ maps the unit cube to the parallelepiped whose edges are the columns of $A$, and $|\det A|$ is the factor by which volume is scaled. The sign tells whether orientation is preserved. If $\det A=0$ the columns are dependent, so the box collapses into a lower-dimensional flat shape with zero volume; $A$ squashes space and cannot be undone, which is why it has no inverse.

m3-l014-eigen-intro.prompt: The rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (a $90^\circ$ rotation) has what eigenvalues, and why?
options: $\pm i$: every real vector is turned, so none keeps its direction.
$+1$ and $-1$, one for each of the two directions it rotates.
Both $0$, since the matrix is singular and has zero trace.
$1$ twice, since a rotation preserves the length of every vector.
m3-l014-eigen-intro.explanation: $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+1=0$. There is no real vector with $Ax=\lambda x$ because $A$ rotates every direction; the complex eigenvalues $\pm i$ encode the rotation. Length preservation shows $|\lambda|=1$, not $\lambda=1$.

m3-l014-eigen-intro.prompt: In Hückel theory, the secular equation $\det(H-E\,I)=0$ is an eigenvalue problem. What do the eigenvectors represent?
options: The number of electrons that occupy each of the molecular orbitals.
The bond lengths between neighbouring atoms in the conjugated chain.
The LCAO coefficients of each carbon $p$ orbital in each molecular orbital.
The nuclear charges of the atoms, which set the orbital energies.
m3-l014-eigen-intro.explanation: Eigenvalues are the orbital energies $E=\alpha+x\beta$; each eigenvector lists the atomic-orbital coefficients $c_i$ of the molecular orbital with that energy. Electron occupation is filled in afterwards.

m3-l014-eigen-intro.prompt: A $3\times3$ matrix has eigenvalues $2$ and $3$ and its trace is $10$. What is its determinant?
m3-l014-eigen-intro.explanation: The trace equals the sum of eigenvalues, so the third is $10-2-3=5$. The determinant is the product: $2\cdot3\cdot5=30$.

m3-l014-eigen-intro.prompt: Explain the geometric meaning of an eigenvector, and what complex eigenvalues or a defective matrix tell you about the transformation.
m3-l014-eigen-intro.rubric: Full credit requires: eigenvector keeps its direction (only stretched/flipped by lambda); complex eigenvalues = rotation component (no real invariant direction); defective = repeated eigenvalue with too few independent eigenvectors so no eigenbasis (shear-like).
m3-l014-eigen-intro.modelAnswer: An eigenvector is a direction that the matrix only stretches (or flips) by the factor $\lambda$ without turning it. If the matrix rotates every real direction, as a rotation does, there are no real eigenvectors and the eigenvalues are complex, carrying the rotation angle and scale. A defective matrix has a repeated eigenvalue but too few independent eigenvectors, so there is no full eigenbasis; a shear is the typical example.

m3-l015-diagonalization.prompt: Which of these matrices cannot be diagonalised?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, because its eigenvalue 2 is repeated.
$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, because its diagonal entries are zero.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which has only one eigenvector.
$\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, because one eigenvalue is negative.
m3-l015-diagonalization.explanation: A matrix is diagonalisable exactly when it has $n$ independent eigenvectors. A repeated eigenvalue is not the problem ($2I$ is already diagonal); the shear has $A-I$ of rank 1, giving only one eigenvector.

m3-l015-diagonalization.prompt: Why does repeatedly applying a Markov (probability-conserving) matrix $A^kx_0$ settle to a steady state?
options: The eigenvalue-1 part survives while the other parts decay away.
Every entry of $A^k$ shrinks to zero, leaving the zero distribution.
All other eigenvalues are exactly zero except for one very large one.
$A^k$ eventually equals the identity matrix, freezing any distribution.
m3-l015-diagonalization.explanation: $A^kx_0=\sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$. With $\lambda_1=1$ and $|\lambda_{i>1}|<1$ only the first term remains: the steady-state distribution (also the equilibrium populations of a kinetic scheme).

m3-l015-diagonalization.prompt: Using $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$ for the Fibonacci matrix, $F_k=(\varphi^k-\psi^k)/\sqrt5$. Estimate $F_{30}$ (use $\varphi^{30}/\sqrt5$, rounded).
m3-l015-diagonalization.explanation: $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\approx1.618$ is the dominant eigenvalue, and $\varphi^{30}/\sqrt5\approx832{,}040$ (the $\psi^k$ term is negligible). Growth rate is set by the largest eigenvalue.

m3-l015-diagonalization.prompt: A two-state system hops with transition matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ (columns sum to 1). In the long-time steady state, what fraction of the population is in state 1?
m3-l015-diagonalization.explanation: The eigenvalue-1 eigenvector satisfies $0.1x_1=0.2x_2$, so $x=(2,1)$ normalised to sum 1 is $(2/3,1/3)$. The fraction is $0.667$.

m3-l015-diagonalization.prompt: Explain why $A^k=S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$ makes powers easy, and how the sizes of the eigenvalues decide whether $A^kx$ grows, decays or settles.
m3-l015-diagonalization.rubric: Full credit requires: in the eigenbasis A acts independently on each coordinate, so powers just raise each eigenvalue to k; $A^kx=\sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$; decays if all $|\lambda|<1$, grows if any $|\lambda|>1$, settles if the largest is exactly 1 and others are smaller.
m3-l015-diagonalization.modelAnswer: Writing $x$ in the eigenvector basis, $A$ just multiplies each component by its eigenvalue, so applying $A$ $k$ times multiplies by $\lambda_i^k$: $A^kx=\sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$. The terms with $|\lambda_i|<1$ decay, those with $|\lambda_i|>1$ grow, and the largest eigenvalue eventually dominates; if it is exactly 1 and the rest are smaller, the vector converges to a steady state.

m3-l016-ode-systems.prompt: The system $\dot u=Au$ has eigenvalues $-1\pm2i$. How do solutions behave?
options: They spiral outward, growing exponentially while they oscillate.
They oscillate forever with constant amplitude, as for a centre.
They decay smoothly without oscillating.
They spiral into the origin, decaying like $e^{-t}$ while oscillating.
m3-l016-ode-systems.explanation: $e^{(-1\pm2i)t}=e^{-t}(\cos2t\pm i\sin2t)$: the imaginary part gives oscillation and the real part gives the decay. Stability depends on the real parts of the eigenvalues.

m3-l016-ode-systems.prompt: For the consecutive first-order reactions $A\xrightarrow{k_1}B\xrightarrow{k_2}C$ written as $\dot u=Au$ (with $u=[A,B,C]$), what are the eigenvalues of $A$?
options: $k_1$, $k_2$ and $k_1+k_2$, the positive rates of the three steps.
$-k_1$, $-k_2$ and $0$, the zero being the all-$C$ end state.
$-k_1-k_2$ only, since the three concentrations decay together.
m3-l016-ode-systems.explanation: The matrix is lower triangular with diagonal $-k_1,-k_2,0$. The rate constants are decay rates (negative eigenvalues), and the zero eigenvalue reflects conservation of total material, with the steady state being pure $C$.

m3-l016-ode-systems.prompt: Turn $y''+3y'+2y=0$, $y(0)=1$, $y'(0)=0$ into a first-order system with $u=(y,y')$ and find $y(1)$.
Explain why $e^{At}=Se^{\Lambda t}S^{-1}$ solves $\dot u=Au$ and how the eigenvalues determine stability.
m3-l016-ode-systems.rubric: Full credit requires: power series of $e^{At}$ and $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$ gives $S e^{\Lambda t}S^{-1}$ (or direct: each eigenvector evolves independently as $e^{\lambda t}$); stability iff all real parts negative; zero real part = neutral (oscillation or constant), any positive real part = growth.
m3-l016-ode-systems.modelAnswer: In the eigenbasis the system decouples into independent equations $\dot c_i=\lambda_ic_i$, each solved by $e^{\lambda_it}$; transforming back gives $u(t)=Se^{\Lambda t}S^{-1}u(0)=e^{At}u(0)$ (equivalently, substitute $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$ into the power series of $e^{At}$). Every mode behaves as $e^{\lambda t}$, so the system decays to zero if all eigenvalues have negative real parts and blows up if any has a positive real part; the imaginary parts only add oscillation.

m3-l017-symmetric.prompt: Two identical masses on springs have force-constant matrix $K=k\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with eigenvalues $k$ (vector $(1,1)$) and $3k$ (vector $(1,-1)$). Which statement is right?
options: The out-of-phase $(1,-1)$ mode is faster, and the two modes are orthogonal.
The in-phase $(1,1)$ mode is faster.
Both modes share one frequency.
The $(1,-1)$ mode is faster, but the modes are not orthogonal because of the coupling.
m3-l017-symmetric.explanation: $\omega^2=\lambda/m$, so the larger eigenvalue $3k$ is the faster mode: the middle spring is stretched and compressed, so the restoring force is larger. The spectral theorem guarantees orthogonal eigenvectors for symmetric $K$.

m3-l017-symmetric.prompt: The quadratic form $x^TSx=1$ has $S$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $4$. What is its shape?
options: An ellipse with semi-axes $1$ and $4$ along the eigenvectors.
A hyperbola, since the two eigenvalues are different from each other.
An ellipse with semi-axes $1$ and $1/2$ along the eigenvectors.
A circle, since $S$ is symmetric and so has no preferred directions.
m3-l017-symmetric.explanation: In the eigenbasis, $\lambda_1y_1^2+\lambda_2y_2^2=1$ has semi-axes $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$: a larger eigenvalue gives a shorter axis. Both eigenvalues positive gives an ellipse.

m3-l017-symmetric.prompt: A symmetric coupled-oscillator problem has $K=k\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with $k=100$ N/m and masses $m=0.5$ kg each. Find the angular frequency $\omega$ of the out-of-phase mode in rad/s.
m3-l017-symmetric.explanation: The eigenvalue is $3k=300$ N/m, so $\omega=\sqrt{300/0.5}=\sqrt{600}\approx24.5$ rad/s. (The in-phase mode has $\omega=\sqrt{200}\approx14.1$ rad/s.)

m3-l017-symmetric.prompt: The Hückel matrix for the allyl system is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (in units of $\beta$). Give the largest eigenvalue.
m3-l017-symmetric.explanation: The eigenvalues are $\sqrt2,0,-\sqrt2$, giving orbital energies $\alpha+\sqrt2\beta$, $\alpha$, $\alpha-\sqrt2\beta$. The largest eigenvalue is $\sqrt2\approx1.414$ (the bonding orbital, since $\beta<0$).

m3-l017-symmetric.prompt: Why are the eigenvectors of a real symmetric matrix for different eigenvalues orthogonal, and why does that matter for normal modes of a molecule?
m3-l017-symmetric.rubric: Full credit requires: argument $\lambda_1 x_1\cdot x_2=Sx_1\cdot x_2=x_1\cdot Sx_2=\lambda_2x_1\cdot x_2$ so $(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)x_1\cdot x_2=0$; consequence: independent, non-interacting modes, each oscillating at its own frequency; eigenvalues give $\omega^2$.
m3-l017-symmetric.modelAnswer: Using symmetry, $\lambda_1(x_1\cdot x_2)=(Sx_1)\cdot x_2=x_1\cdot(Sx_2)=\lambda_2(x_1\cdot x_2)$, so if $\lambda_1\ne\lambda_2$ the dot product must be zero. For vibrations this means the normal modes form an orthogonal set of independent motions: energy put into one mode stays in it, each mode oscillating at its own frequency $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda/m}$, and any motion is a superposition of them.

m3-l018-positive-definite.prompt: Which of these symmetric matrices is positive definite?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, since all of its entries are positive.
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $1,3$ and pivots $2,1.5$.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, since its entries are positive and increasing.
$\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, since its determinant $2$ is positive.
m3-l018-positive-definite.explanation: Positive entries are not enough: the second and third matrices have determinants $-3$ and $-1$ (a negative eigenvalue). The last has $\det>0$ but both eigenvalues negative. Positive definite needs all eigenvalues (or pivots) positive.

m3-l018-positive-definite.prompt: A critical point of a potential energy surface has a Hessian with eigenvalues $+2$ and $-3$ (in some units). What is the point?
options: A local minimum, because at least one eigenvalue is positive.
A local maximum, because the larger-magnitude eigenvalue is negative.
Inconclusive, because a Hessian alone cannot classify a critical point.
A saddle point, as for a chemical transition state.
m3-l018-positive-definite.explanation: A minimum needs all Hessian eigenvalues positive, a maximum all negative, mixed signs give a saddle. A transition state is a first-order saddle with exactly one negative eigenvalue (the reaction coordinate).

m3-l018-positive-definite.prompt: For the symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, elimination gives pivots $2,\ 3/2,\ ?$. What is the third pivot?
m3-l018-positive-definite.explanation: The pivots are $2,\tfrac32,\tfrac43$, all positive, so the matrix is positive definite. The product $2\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac43=4=\det$.

m3-l018-positive-definite.prompt: The quadratic form $f=x^2+4xy+c\,y^2$ has a minimum at the origin only if $c$ exceeds a threshold. What is that value of $c$?
m3-l018-positive-definite.explanation: $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&c\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=c-4$, which must be positive (with $S_{11}=1>0$), so $c>4$. At $c=4$ the form is only semidefinite.

m3-l018-positive-definite.prompt: Why is $A^TA$ always positive semidefinite, and why is that relevant to least-squares fitting?
m3-l018-positive-definite.rubric: Full credit requires: $x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|^2\ge0$; positive definite when columns independent ($Ax=0$ only for $x=0$); the least-squares cost $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is a quadratic with Hessian $2A^TA$, so it has a unique minimum (a bowl) when A has independent columns.
m3-l018-positive-definite.modelAnswer: For any $x$, $x^TA^TAx=(Ax)\cdot(Ax)=\|Ax\|^2\ge0$, so $A^TA$ is positive semidefinite; it is strictly positive when $Ax=0$ only for $x=0$, i.e. independent columns. The least-squares error $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is a quadratic function of $x$ with Hessian $2A^TA$, so independent columns make it a bowl with a single minimum at the solution of the normal equations.

m3-l019-complex-vectors.prompt: For $z=(1,i)$, the plain transpose gives $z^Tz=1+i^2=0$ even though $z\ne0$. What fixes this?
options: Restrict attention to vectors whose components are all real numbers.
Use the conjugate transpose: $\|z\|^2=z^Hz=\sum|z_k|^2$.
Take the absolute value of $z^Tz$ after multiplying out the terms.
Use $z^Tz$ as before, but only for vectors normalised to unit length.
m3-l019-complex-vectors.explanation: A length must be real and positive. Conjugating one factor makes each term $\bar z_kz_k=|z_k|^2\ge0$, so $z^Hz=0$ only for $z=0$. For $z=(1,i)$, $z^Hz=2$.

m3-l019-complex-vectors.prompt: In bra-ket notation, what matrix object is the bra $\langle\psi|$ when $|\psi\rangle$ is a column vector?
options: The plain transpose of the column, with no complex conjugation applied.
The complex-conjugate column, conjugated entry by entry but not turned.
The matrix inverse of the ket, chosen so that $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1$.
The conjugate-transpose row, so $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle=\psi^H\phi$.
m3-l019-complex-vectors.explanation: Bras are conjugate-transpose rows, so $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=\sum|\psi_k|^2$ is a probability-like norm. The inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot, so $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle=\overline{\langle\phi|\psi\rangle}$.

m3-l019-complex-vectors.prompt: Why does the correct inner product for complex vectors use a conjugate, what rule replaces $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$, and how does it connect to bra-ket notation?
m3-l019-complex-vectors.rubric: Full credit requires: conjugate needed so that length squared is real/positive; $(AB)^H=B^HA^H$; $|\psi\rangle$ = column, $\langle\psi|$ = conjugate row; $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$ is the same Hermitian inner product (complex number, conjugate when swapped).
m3-l019-complex-vectors.modelAnswer: Without conjugation a nonzero complex vector can have zero or complex 'length', so we conjugate one vector: $\langle z,w\rangle=z^Hw$, giving $\|z\|^2=\sum|z_k|^2>0$. For products, $(AB)^H=B^HA^H$: transpose and conjugate. A physicist's ket $|\psi\rangle$ is the column, the bra $\langle\psi|$ is its conjugate-transpose row, and $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$ is exactly $\psi^H\phi$, the overlap of two states.

m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes quantum mechanics?
options: Observables are Hermitian, and time evolution is unitary.
Observables are unitary, and time evolution is Hermitian.
Both observables and time evolution are Hermitian matrices acting on states.
Observables can be any real matrix, and time evolution any invertible matrix.
m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.explanation: Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues, which are the possible measurement results. Unitary matrices preserve $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$, so $e^{-iHt/\hbar}$ keeps total probability equal to 1.

m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.prompt: The Pauli matrices are both Hermitian and unitary. What must their eigenvalues be?
options: $+i$ or $-i$, like a rotation through $90^\circ$ in the plane.
Any real numbers at all.
Only $+1$ or $-1$: real, and of modulus one.
$0$ or $1$, as for projection operators onto a subspace.
m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.explanation: Real and modulus 1 leaves $\pm1$. Hence a spin-1/2 measurement along any axis gives one of two outcomes (in units of $\hbar/2$).

m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.prompt: Find the larger eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix $H=\begin{pmatrix}1&1-i\\1+i&2\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.explanation: Trace $=3$ and $\det=2-|1-i|^2=2-2=0$, so the eigenvalues are $0$ and $3$ (real, as Hermitian demands).

m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.prompt: A spin starts in $|0\rangle$ and evolves under the unitary $U=e^{i\theta\sigma_x}=\cos\theta\,I+i\sin\theta\,\sigma_x$ with $\theta=\pi/6$. What is the probability to find it in $|1\rangle$?
m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.explanation: $U|0\rangle=\cos\theta|0\rangle+i\sin\theta|1\rangle$, so $P(1)=\sin^2(\pi/6)=0.25$. Probabilities still add to 1 because $U$ is unitary.

m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.prompt: Explain why a Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, and why $e^{-iHt}$ is unitary when $H$ is Hermitian.
m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.rubric: Full credit requires: $\lambda\|x\|^2=x^HHx$ is real since $(x^HHx)^*=x^HH^Hx=x^HHx$; orthogonality by the same swap argument; $U=e^{-iHt}$ has $U^HU=e^{iHt}e^{-iHt}=I$ (or eigenvalues $e^{-i\lambda t}$ of modulus 1).
m3-l020-hermitian-unitary.modelAnswer: For $Hx=\lambda x$, the number $x^HHx=\lambda\|x\|^2$ equals its own conjugate because $H=H^H$, so $\lambda$ is real; the same swap shows eigenvectors with different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Writing $H=U\Lambda U^H$, $e^{-iHt}=Ue^{-i\Lambda t}U^H$ has eigenvalues $e^{-i\lambda t}$ of modulus one, and $(e^{-iHt})^H e^{-iHt}=e^{iHt}e^{-iHt}=I$, so it preserves probability.

m3-l021-fft.prompt: What is the key idea that lets the FFT compute an $n$-point DFT in about $n\log_2 n$ operations instead of $n^2$?
options: It discards the small Fourier coefficients and computes only the large ones.
It works only for real signals.
$F_n$ factors into sparse matrices built from half-size transforms.
It uses the inverse matrix.
m3-l021-fft.explanation: The FFT is exact, not approximate. Splitting by even/odd indices reduces one size-$n$ transform to two size-$n/2$ transforms plus $O(n)$ work, and recursion over $\log_2n$ levels gives $O(n\log n)$.

m3-l021-fft.prompt: What does it mean that $F_n/\sqrt n$ is a unitary matrix?
options: Its columns are orthonormal complex exponentials, so its inverse is $F^H$.
Its columns are real vectors of unit length that point along coordinate axes.
Its entries all have modulus $1/n$.
It is symmetric, so it is its own inverse and the transform is an involution.
m3-l021-fft.explanation: The columns $(1,\omega^k,\omega^{2k},\dots)/\sqrt n$ are orthonormal under the Hermitian inner product, so $F^HF=nI$. This is why Fourier expansion works like any orthonormal-basis expansion, and inverting costs the same as the forward transform.

m3-l021-fft.prompt: Compare the cost of a direct DFT ($n^2$) with an FFT ($n\log_2n$) for $n=1024$. By what factor is the FFT faster?
A signal $x_j=\cos(2\pi\cdot2\,j/8)$, $j=0..7$, is Fourier transformed with an 8-point DFT. What is the magnitude of the coefficient at frequency index $k=2$?
m3-l021-fft.explanation: $\cos$ is half of $e^{2\pi i2j/8}$ plus half of its conjugate; the DFT sums 8 terms of size $1/2$ aligned in phase, giving magnitude $8/2=4$ at $k=2$ (and $k=6$).

m3-l021-fft.prompt: Interpret the discrete Fourier transform as an expansion in an orthonormal basis, and say in words why splitting into even and odd samples saves work.
m3-l021-fft.rubric: Full credit requires: DFT coefficients = inner products with orthonormal complex exponentials (signal rewritten as a sum of them); even/odd split: two half-size DFTs reuse shared structure ($\omega^2$ is the primitive root for n/2), repeated recursively -> n log n.
m3-l021-fft.modelAnswer: The DFT finds how much of each complex exponential is in a sampled signal; because those exponentials form an orthonormal basis, the coefficients are just inner products and the original signal is recovered by summing the basis vectors back up. The FFT notices that the even-indexed and odd-indexed samples each form a half-size DFT using the same exponentials squared, so one size-$n$ transform becomes two size-$n/2$ transforms plus a linear pass; recursing $\log_2n$ times costs $n\log n$ instead of $n^2$.

m3-l022-svd.prompt: Geometrically, what does $A=U\Sigma V^T$ do to the unit circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: A larger circle, scaled by the largest eigenvalue of $A$ in every direction.
An ellipse whose semi-axes are always the eigenvalues of $A$ itself.
A line segment of length $\det A$, since the matrix compresses the circle.
It becomes an ellipse whose semi-axes are $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$.
m3-l022-svd.explanation: Every matrix maps the unit circle to an ellipse (possibly degenerate). The semi-axis lengths are the singular values, which agree with eigenvalues only for symmetric positive semidefinite matrices.

m3-l022-svd.prompt: How do you obtain the singular values and right singular vectors of $A$?
options: From the eigenproblem of $A$ itself, where the eigenvalues are the $\sigma_i$.
From $A^TA$: its eigenvectors give $V$ and its eigenvalues give $\sigma_i^2$.
From the eigenproblem of $A+A^T$, which is always symmetric and real.
From the pivots that elimination finds when it reduces $A$ to echelon form.
m3-l022-svd.explanation: $A^TA=V\Sigma^TU^TU\Sigma V^T=V\Sigma^2V^T$, a symmetric eigenproblem that exists for every matrix, even rectangular or defective ones. Then $u_i=Av_i/\sigma_i$.

m3-l022-svd.prompt: Find the largest singular value of $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l022-svd.explanation: $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}25&20\\20&25\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $45$ and $5$, so $\sigma=\sqrt{45}\approx6.708$ and $\sqrt5$. Note $\sigma_1\sigma_2=15=|\det A|$.

m3-l022-svd.prompt: The rank-one matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has one nonzero singular value. What is it?
Explain how the SVD hands you orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces.
m3-l022-svd.rubric: Full credit requires: first r columns of V = row space, remaining n-r = nullspace; first r columns of U = column space, remaining m-r = left nullspace; $Av_i=\sigma_iu_i$ ties them together.
m3-l022-svd.modelAnswer: In $A=U\Sigma V^T$, the first $r$ columns of $V$ (with nonzero $\sigma_i$) form an orthonormal basis for the row space, and the remaining $n-r$ columns span the nullspace since $Av_i=0$ there. Likewise the first $r$ columns of $U$ form a basis for the column space and the last $m-r$ for the left nullspace. $A$ maps $v_i\to\sigma_iu_i$, pairing a row-space direction with a column-space direction.

m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.prompt: A data matrix has singular values $10, 5, 0.1, 0.01$. Why is the rank-2 truncation a good approximation?
options: The error is the next singular value, $0.1$, small against $10$ and $5$.
Because the first two singular values are both larger than one.
Because the rank-2 approximation is exact for any matrix with 4 columns.
Because the smallest singular values carry the main information in the data.
m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.explanation: The truncated SVD $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^T$ is the closest rank-$k$ matrix, with 2-norm error $\sigma_{k+1}$. Large singular values carry the dominant structure (e.g. component spectra); tiny ones are typically noise.

m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.prompt: A matrix has singular values $1000$ and $0.001$. What does its condition number $\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}=10^6$ tell you?
options: It is invertible, with an inverse whose norm is exactly $0.001$.
It has rank $10^6$, which makes the system hugely over-determined.
Relative errors can be amplified up to $10^6$ times in the solution.
Computations are accurate, because the largest singular value is large.
m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.explanation: Dividing by $\sigma_{\min}$ magnifies tiny errors in the corresponding direction. Large condition numbers signal near-dependent columns (e.g. strongly overlapping spectra in a calibration).

m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.prompt: Compute the condition number $\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$ of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4.01\end{pmatrix}$ (nearly singular). Give the value to a few significant figures.
m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.explanation: The singular values are about $5.01$ and $0.002$, so the condition number is roughly $2.5\times10^3$. Nearly dependent columns make solving $Ax=b$ very sensitive.

m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.prompt: In a PCA of a spectral data set the singular values are $6,\,3,\,2$. What percentage of the total variance (sum of $\sigma_i^2$) does the first principal component capture?
m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.explanation: Variance scales as $\sigma^2$: $36/(36+9+4)=36/49\approx73.5\%$. Two components capture $45/49\approx92\%$.

m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.prompt: What does the pseudoinverse $A^+=V\Sigma^+U^T$ give you, and how would SVD or PCA help you analyse a set of spectra of mixtures?
m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.rubric: Full credit requires: $A^+b$ is the least-squares solution of smallest norm (inverts nonzero $\sigma$, ignores zero ones, lies in the row space); spectra: SVD/PCA finds a few dominant components (rank = number of independent species), the rest is noise; centre data first for PCA.
m3-l023-svd-pca-pinv.modelAnswer: $A^+$ inverts $A$ only on the directions it actually uses (dividing by nonzero $\sigma_i$) and ignores the rest, so $A^+b$ is the least-squares solution that also has the smallest length, even when $A$ is rank-deficient or rectangular. For a data set of mixture spectra the SVD finds the few orthogonal spectral components that explain nearly all the variance; the number of large singular values estimates how many independent absorbing species are present, and the small ones are noise.

m3-l024-linear-transformations.prompt: Which of these maps of the plane to itself is NOT a linear transformation?
options: Rotation by $30^\circ$ about the origin of the plane.
Translation by $(1,0)$, which moves the origin so cannot be linear.
Orthogonal projection onto the $x$-axis of the plane.
Reflection across the line $y=x$ in the plane.
m3-l024-linear-transformations.explanation: Linearity requires $T(0)=0$ (and $T(cv)=cT(v)$, $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$). Translation moves the origin, so it fails; it is an affine, not linear, map.

m3-l024-linear-transformations.prompt: Transformation $T$ has matrix $A$ and $S$ has matrix $B$ (same basis). What is the matrix of 'apply $T$ first, then $S$'?
options: $AB$, because the first transformation is written first.
$A+B$, because transformations add.
$B^{-1}A$, because $S$ must be undone.
$BA$, since the vector meets $A$ first: $S(T(v))=B(Av)$.
m3-l024-linear-transformations.explanation: Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication with the later transformation on the left. That is the origin of the non-commutativity of successive rotations.

m3-l024-linear-transformations.prompt: Let $D=d/dx$ act on polynomials of degree $\le2$ with basis $\{1,x,x^2\}$. The matrix of $D$ has columns $D(1),D(x),D(x^2)$ written in the basis. Give the entry in row 2, column 3.
m3-l024-linear-transformations.explanation: $D(x^2)=2x=0\cdot1+2\cdot x+0\cdot x^2$, so column 3 is $(0,2,0)^T$ and the $(2,3)$ entry is 2. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has nullspace spanned by the constant.

m3-l024-linear-transformations.prompt: What is the dimension of the kernel of $d^2/dx^2$ acting on polynomials of degree $\le4$?
m3-l024-linear-transformations.explanation: $p''=0$ gives $p=a+bx$, a 2-dimensional kernel. The range is the polynomials of degree $\le2$ (dimension 3); $2+3=5=\dim$ of the input space.

m3-l024-linear-transformations.prompt: Explain how to build the matrix of a linear transformation from its action on a basis, and how the kernel and range relate to the nullspace and column space.
m3-l024-linear-transformations.rubric: Full credit requires: column j = coordinates of $T(\text{basis vector}_j)$ in the output basis (linearity then determines T everywhere); kernel = vectors mapped to 0 = nullspace of the matrix; range = span of the images = column space; the matrix depends on the chosen bases.
m3-l024-linear-transformations.modelAnswer: Because $T$ is linear, knowing what it does to each input basis vector determines it completely: write each image $T(v_j)$ in the output basis and use those coordinates as column $j$. Then the coordinates of $T(x)$ are $A$ times the coordinates of $x$. The kernel (inputs sent to zero) is the nullspace of $A$, and the range (all outputs) is spanned by the images, i.e. the column space; the entries change with the choice of bases but these subspaces are intrinsic.

m3-l025-change-of-basis.prompt: $B=M^{-1}AM$ is similar to $A$. Which quantity is NOT necessarily the same for $A$ and $B$?
options: The eigenvalues, which are intrinsic to the transformation itself.
The eigenvectors, whose coordinate lists change with the basis.
The trace, which equals the sum of the eigenvalues in any basis.
The determinant, which is the product of the eigenvalues in any basis.
m3-l025-change-of-basis.explanation: Similar matrices represent the same transformation in different bases, so eigenvalues, trace and determinant (all intrinsic) agree. Eigenvectors are the same geometric directions but their coordinate lists differ: $x_B=M^{-1}x_A$.

options: Its eigenvalues are complex, so no real eigenbasis can be formed.
It is not symmetric, and only symmetric matrices can be diagonalised.
Its determinant is nonzero.
The eigenvalue 2 is repeated, yet there is only one eigenvector.
m3-l025-change-of-basis.explanation: $A-2I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has a one-dimensional nullspace, so there is one eigenvector. Many nonsymmetric matrices are diagonalisable; the issue is the count of independent eigenvectors.

m3-l025-change-of-basis.prompt: Express $v=(3,1)$ in the basis $b_1=(1,1)$, $b_2=(1,-1)$, i.e. find $c_1,c_2$ with $v=c_1b_1+c_2b_2$. Give $c_1$.
m3-l025-change-of-basis.explanation: Solve $c_1+c_2=3$, $c_1-c_2=1$: $c_1=2$, $c_2=1$. In general the coordinates are $M^{-1}v$ where $M$ has the basis vectors as columns.

m3-l025-change-of-basis.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(2,2)$ entry of $B=M^{-1}AM$.
m3-l025-change-of-basis.explanation: $AM=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, $M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ (diagonal: the columns of $M$ are the eigenvectors). The $(2,2)$ entry is $3$.

m3-l025-change-of-basis.prompt: Explain diagonalisation as 'choosing the eigenbasis', and why symmetric or Hermitian matrices always admit an orthonormal eigenbasis while a defective matrix does not admit any.
m3-l025-change-of-basis.rubric: Full credit requires: in the eigenbasis the transformation acts as independent stretches (diagonal matrix $\Lambda=S^{-1}AS$); spectral theorem for symmetric/Hermitian; defective = not enough eigenvectors, only a Jordan block (eigenvalue plus a nilpotent shear) is achievable.
m3-l025-change-of-basis.modelAnswer: If we use eigenvectors as the coordinate directions, $A$ just stretches each coordinate by its eigenvalue, so the matrix is diagonal: $\Lambda=S^{-1}AS$. Symmetric/Hermitian matrices always have a full set of mutually orthogonal eigenvectors (spectral theorem), so the basis can be chosen orthonormal. A defective matrix has a repeated eigenvalue without enough independent eigenvectors, so the best one can do is a Jordan form: the eigenvalue on the diagonal plus a 1 above it, which represents a stretch combined with a shear.

m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.prompt: With the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-1}^{1}fg\,dx$, which pair of functions is orthogonal?
options: $x$ and $x^2$, because $x^3$ is odd and its integral over $[-1,1]$ is zero.
$1$ and $x^2$, because one is constant and the other is even.
$x$ and $x$, because a function is always orthogonal to itself.
$1$ and $1$, because the constant function is the simplest vector.
m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.explanation: $\int_{-1}^{1}x^3dx=0$. But $\int 1\cdot x^2dx=2/3\ne0$ and a nonzero function is never orthogonal to itself ($\langle f,f\rangle=\int f^2>0$). Gram-Schmidt on $1,x,x^2$ then yields Legendre polynomials.

m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.prompt: Why are eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint (Hermitian) operator with different eigenvalues orthogonal?
options: Eigenfunctions are always chosen to be sines and cosines of the variable.
Differential operators always have orthogonal solutions, whatever their form.
Self-adjointness gives $(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\langle f_1,f_2\rangle=0$.
Eigenvalues are defined to be orthogonal when they are distinct numbers.
m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.explanation: The proof is the same as for Hermitian matrices, with the inner product replaced by an integral. It is why energy eigenfunctions of different energies are orthogonal in quantum mechanics.

m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.prompt: Run Gram-Schmidt on $\{1,x,x^2\}$ on $[-1,1]$ with weight 1. The second orthogonal polynomial is $x^2-c$. What is $c$?
m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.explanation: $c=\langle x^2,1\rangle/\langle1,1\rangle=(2/3)/2=1/3$, giving $x^2-\tfrac13\propto P_2(x)$ (with $x$ already orthogonal to both by parity).

m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.prompt: Project $f=x^3$ onto $x$ in this function space: find $\langle x^3,x\rangle/\langle x,x\rangle$ on $[-1,1]$.
m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.explanation: $\int x^4dx=2/5$ and $\int x^2dx=2/3$, so the coefficient is $(2/5)/(2/3)=3/5=0.6$. The remainder $x^3-\tfrac35x$ is orthogonal to $x$ (it is proportional to $P_3$).

m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.prompt: What is the analogy between functions and vectors, and between Hermitian matrices and self-adjoint operators, that lets us treat Fourier or Legendre expansions as 'projection onto a basis'?
m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.rubric: Full credit requires: functions as vectors in a space with inner product $\int fg$; orthogonal basis functions with coefficients = inner products ($\langle f,\phi_n\rangle/\langle\phi_n,\phi_n\rangle$); self-adjoint operator ~ Hermitian matrix with real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenfunctions, so an expansion is a change of basis.
m3-l026-inner-product-spaces.modelAnswer: A function can be thought of as an infinite list of values, with an inner product $\int f^*g$ playing the role of the dot product. Then a set of orthogonal functions such as sines or Legendre polynomials is an orthogonal basis, and the expansion coefficient of $f$ is the projection $\langle f,\phi_n\rangle/\langle\phi_n,\phi_n\rangle$, just as with vectors. Self-adjoint differential operators play the role of Hermitian matrices, with real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenfunctions, which supplies the natural bases.

m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.prompt: Two Hermitian matrices $A$ and $B$ satisfy $AB=BA$. What follows?
options: They must have exactly the same set of eigenvalues as each other.
They must be scalar multiples of one another.
They share a complete orthonormal set of eigenvectors.
Nothing can be said about their eigenvectors without more information.
m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.explanation: If $Ax=\lambda x$ then $B(Ax)=A(Bx)$ means $Bx$ is also in the eigenspace of $\lambda$, so $B$ can be diagonalised within each eigenspace. They need not have the same eigenvalues, only the same eigenvectors.

m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.prompt: The spin operators $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_z$ do not commute. What does this mean physically?
options: No state has definite values of both, and an uncertainty relation applies.
Both can be measured to any precision, but only in a fixed order.
Neither operator has eigenvalues, so neither can be measured at all.
They describe the same measurement made in two different unit systems.
m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.explanation: Commuting observables share eigenstates, so definite values for both are possible. Non-commuting ones have no common eigenbasis, which is the matrix-level origin of the uncertainty principle.

m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.prompt: Compute the commutator $[A,B]=AB-BA$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and give its $(1,2)$ entry.
m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.explanation: $AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $[A,B]=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$. This is $-2i\sigma_y$, consistent with $[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]=-2i\sigma_y$.

m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.prompt: A molecule has 5 coupled spin-1/2 nuclei. What is the dimension of its spin Hilbert space (the Kronecker product of five $2\times2$ spaces)?
m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.explanation: Dimensions multiply: $2^5=32$. The spin Hamiltonian is a $32\times32$ Hermitian matrix built from Kronecker products, which is why simulating NMR of large spin systems grows costly.

m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.prompt: Explain why commuting observables can be measured simultaneously, and how a two-spin Hilbert space is built from a Kronecker product.
m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.rubric: Full credit requires: commuting Hermitian operators share eigenvectors, so a state can have definite values of both; for two spins, basis states are $|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle$ (dimension $2\times2=4$) and an operator on spin 1 alone is $A\otimes I$, on spin 2 alone $I\otimes B$ (Kronecker products).
m3-l027-commuting-operators-tensor.modelAnswer: If two Hermitian operators commute they can be diagonalised together, so there are states that are simultaneously eigenstates of both and a measurement of one does not disturb the other. For two spin-1/2 particles the joint state space has basis $|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle$, dimension $4$; an operator acting only on spin 1 is $A\otimes I$ and one acting only on spin 2 is $I\otimes B$, and these commute, as operators on different spins should. A coupled-spin Hamiltonian is a sum of such Kronecker products.
